chapter.subject: computer-networks

topics.title: Chapter frame: four issues the chapter must cover

sourceRefs.evidence: This chapter addresses four issues: data communications, networks, the Internet, and protocols and standards.

learningObjectives: State the four issues the chapter addresses
Place later sections on that roadmap

concepts.title: Four chapter pillars
concepts.meaning: Data communications, networks, the Internet, protocols and standards.

explanation.what: The source explicitly organizes Chapter 1 around four sequential issues.
explanation.why: Gives students a scaffold before dense definitions.
explanation.concrete: Broad definition of data communications → networks as a highway → Internet as internetwork example → protocol vs standard.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Low direct exam value, high structural value for chapter coherence.

relationships.explanation: Chapter introduces data communications first, then networks, Internet, protocols/standards.

preservationRequirements: Open with the four-issue roadmap so later sections are not orphaned facts.

acceptable: Name the four issues in one short roadmap paragraph.
notAcceptable: Drop the roadmap and jump straight into Shannon-style formulas.

topics.title: Data communications: definition, effectiveness, five components

sourceRefs.evidence: Data communications are the exchange of data between two devices via some form of transmission medium.

learningObjectives: Define data communications and data
List the four effectiveness characteristics including jitter
Name and explain the five components
Use the protocol analogy to explain why connection ≠ communication

concepts.title: Data
concepts.meaning: Information presented in whatever form is agreed upon by the parties creating and using the data.

explanation.what: Data is agreed-form information, not merely 'numbers'.
explanation.why: Without an agreed form, bits cannot be interpreted.
explanation.concrete: Text, numbers, pictures, audio, video are popular message forms.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Foundational term; appears in definitions and component lists.

sourceRefs.evidence: The word data refers to information presented in whatever form is agreed upon by the parties creating and using the data.

concepts.title: Telecommunication
concepts.meaning: Communication at a distance (telephony, telegraphy, television).

explanation.what: tele = Greek for 'far'; includes telephony, telegraphy, television.
explanation.why: Separates remote communication from face-to-face local communication.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Occasional vocabulary item; not a computation target.

concepts.title: Data communications
concepts.meaning: Exchange of data between two devices via some form of transmission medium such as a wire cable.

explanation.what: Two-device exchange over a medium, requiring a hardware+software communication system.
explanation.why: Defines the chapter's first pillar.
explanation.how: Devices participate in a communication system made of hardware (physical equipment) and software (programs).
explanation.notMeaning: Not merely 'sending a file'; not the same as networking topology.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Core definition; review Q1 builds on the five components of this system.

sourceRefs.evidence: Data communications are the exchange of data between two devices via some form of transmission medium.

concepts.title: Effectiveness characteristics
concepts.meaning: Delivery, accuracy, timeliness, and jitter determine data-communications effectiveness.

explanation.what: Four fundamental characteristics of an effective system.
explanation.why: Correct destination without accuracy or timing is still useless.
explanation.whenChanges: If any one fails, the communication is ineffective for real applications.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Direct source emphasis; easy multiple-choice set.

sourceRefs.evidence: The effectiveness of a data communications system depends on four fundamental characteristics: delivery, accuracy, timeliness, and jitter.

concepts.title: Delivery
concepts.meaning: System must deliver data to the correct destination — intended device/user and only that one.

explanation.why: Misdelivery is a security and correctness failure.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Part of the four-characteristic set.

concepts.title: Accuracy
concepts.meaning: System must deliver data accurately; altered-and-uncorrected data are unusable.

explanation.notMeaning: Not the same as timeliness — late-but-correct is still a different failure mode.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Part of the four-characteristic set.

concepts.title: Timeliness
concepts.meaning: Data delivered late are useless; for audio/video this means real-time transmission.

explanation.what: On-time delivery; real-time = as produced, same order, without significant delay.
explanation.why: Interactive media fail without timing even if bits are correct.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Part of the four-characteristic set; links to jitter.

concepts.title: Jitter
concepts.meaning: Variation in packet arrival time — uneven delay in audio/video packet delivery.

explanation.what: Inconsistent inter-arrival times produce uneven quality.
explanation.why: Constant average delay is not enough if delay varies packet-to-packet.
explanation.concrete: Packets sent every 30 ms; some arrive with 30 ms delay, others 40 ms → uneven video.
explanation.notMeaning: Not simply 'high delay'; it is delay variation.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Explicitly defined with a numeric illustration; frequently dropped by summarizers.

sourceRefs.evidence: Jitter refers to the variation in the packet arrival time.

concepts.title: Real-time transmission
concepts.meaning: Timely delivery of audio/video as produced, in order, without significant delay.

explanation.what: Special case of timeliness for continuous media.
explanation.how: Packets must keep production pace and ordering.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Often paired with jitter questions.

concepts.title: Five components of a data communications system
concepts.meaning: Message, sender, receiver, transmission medium, protocol.

explanation.why: Protocol is a component — connection without rules does not communicate.
explanation.concrete: French speaker vs Japanese speaker: connected but not communicating without a shared protocol.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Review Q1 asks students to identify the five components.

sourceRefs.evidence: A data communications system has five components.

concepts.title: Message
concepts.meaning: The information (data) to be communicated.
concepts.whyExamRelevant: Component #1 in the five-part taxonomy.

concepts.title: Sender
concepts.meaning: Device that sends the data message.

explanation.concrete: Computer, workstation, telephone handset, video camera.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Component #2.

concepts.title: Receiver
concepts.meaning: Device that receives the message.

explanation.concrete: Computer, workstation, telephone handset, television.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Component #3.

concepts.title: Transmission medium
concepts.meaning: Physical path by which a message travels from sender to receiver.

explanation.concrete: Twisted-pair wire, coaxial cable, fiber-optic cable, radio waves.
explanation.notMeaning: Not the same as protocol; medium is the path, protocol is the ruleset.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Component #4; media examples are common MCQs.

concepts.title: Protocol (basic role in data communications)
concepts.meaning: Set of rules that govern data communications; agreement between communicating devices.

explanation.what: Without a protocol, two devices may be connected but not communicating.
explanation.why: Shared rules enable interpretation of bits.
explanation.concrete: French speaker cannot understand a Japanese-only speaker.
explanation.notMeaning: Not a physical device; it is a ruleset (component #5).

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Component #5; also the bridge to section 1.4.

sourceRefs.evidence: A protocol is a set of rules that govern data communications.

relationships.explanation: Effectiveness characteristics evaluate whether data communications succeed.
The five components make up the communication system.
Jitter is variation that breaks even when average delay looks acceptable.
Medium is physical path; protocol is governing rules. Both are required components.

definitions.definition: Exchange of data between two devices via some form of transmission medium such as a wire cable.
definitions.qualifier: Effectiveness depends on delivery, accuracy, timeliness, jitter

definitions.definition: Variation in the packet arrival time (uneven delay in audio/video packets).
A set of rules that govern data communications; an agreement between communicating devices.
definitions.qualifier: Connection without protocol does not imply communication

examples.title: Jitter with 30 ms packet interval
examples.scenario: Video packets are produced every 30 ms.
inputs: some packets arrive with 30 ms delay
reasoning: Arrival times vary around the production interval.
Variable delay produces uneven quality even if mean delay is acceptable.
examples.lesson: Timeliness for media includes stability of delay, not only average latency.

sourceRefs.evidence: let us assume that video packets are sent every 30 ms

examples.title: French/Japanese protocol analogy
examples.scenario: Two devices (or people) physically connected but without shared rules.
reasoning: Physical connectivity is insufficient without a shared protocol.
examples.lesson: Protocol is a necessary component, not an optional software add-on.

comparisons.title: Delivery vs Accuracy vs Timeliness vs Jitter
similarities: All four are required for effectiveness.
comparisons.commonTrap: Treating jitter as synonym of delay.

confusions.whyConfused: Both relate to timing of packet arrival.
confusions.correctDistinction: Delay is how long; jitter is how much that long varies.
confusions.examTrap: Selecting 'high delay' when the question describes uneven arrival times.

sourceRefs.evidence: Identify the five components of a data communications system.

preservationRequirements: All five components as a complete set (never drop protocol).
Four effectiveness characteristics including jitter with the 30/40 ms example.
Connected ≠ communicating analogy.

acceptable: Five components are message, sender, receiver, medium, protocol.

topics.title: Data representation: text, numbers, images, audio, video

sourceRefs.evidence: Information today comes in different forms such as text, numbers, images, audio, and video.

learningObjectives: Explain bit-pattern representation of text and numbers
Relate Unicode and ASCII as stated in the source
Describe images as pixel matrices with bit-depth color
Distinguish continuous vs discrete audio/video

concepts.title: Bit pattern representation
concepts.meaning: Text and numbers are represented as sequences of bits (0s or 1s).

explanation.what: Digital systems encode information as bit sequences.
explanation.why: Computers process bits; agreed codes make symbols meaningful.
explanation.how: Codes map symbols to bit patterns; coding is the representation process.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Foundation for Unicode/ASCII and pixel questions (ex. 14–15).

concepts.title: Code and coding
concepts.meaning: A code is a set of bit patterns for text symbols; coding is representing symbols with those patterns.

explanation.concrete: Unicode and ASCII are codes.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Vocabulary used when defining Unicode/ASCII.

concepts.title: Unicode and ASCII (as stated in source)
concepts.meaning: Unicode uses 32 bits (this source) to represent a symbol/character used in any language; ASCII is the first 127 characters / Basic Latin.

explanation.why: World-language coverage vs older US-centric code.
explanation.how: ASCII constitutes the first 127 Unicode characters (Basic Latin).
explanation.notMeaning: This extract states 32-bit Unicode — do not silently 'correct' to UTF-8/UTF-16 without marking EXTERNAL_CONTEXT.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Exercise 14 asks maximum Unicode character/symbol capacity in this framing.

sourceRefs.evidence: Unicode, which uses 32 bits to represent a symbol or character

concepts.title: Numbers as binary values
concepts.meaning: Numbers are bit patterns but not via ASCII; the number is converted directly to binary to simplify math.

explanation.what: Numeric encoding differs from textual digit encoding.
explanation.why: Direct binary conversion simplifies mathematical operations.
explanation.notMeaning: ASCII is not used to represent numbers in this source's account.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Clarifies why '123' as text ≠ 123 as number.

concepts.title: Images as pixel matrices
concepts.meaning: An image is a matrix of pixels; each pixel has a bit pattern whose size/value depend on color depth and content.

explanation.what: Resolution vs memory tradeoff; black-white needs 1 bit; gray levels need more bits; RGB mixes red/green/blue.
explanation.how: 1000 vs 10000 pixels → better resolution, more memory.
explanation.whenChanges: More gray levels or colors ⇒ more bits per pixel ⇒ more memory.
explanation.concrete: 4 gray levels = 2-bit patterns: 00 black, 01 dark gray, 10 light gray, 11 white.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Exercise 15: 16 bits/pixel max colors.

concepts.title: Audio/video continuous vs discrete
concepts.meaning: Audio from a microphone is continuous; video can be continuous (camera) or a sequence of images. Both can later become digital or analog signals.

explanation.how: Chapters 4–5 (forward ref) cover changing sound/video to digital or analog.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Supports real-time/jitter context; not a heavy computation area in Ch.1.

relationships.explanation: ASCII is the first 127 Unicode characters (Basic Latin) in this source.
Pixel color/gray encoding uses bit patterns; depth determines representable values.

definitions.definition: Coding system using 32 bits (per this source) to represent a symbol or character used in any language.
definitions.qualifier: Source states 32-bit; preserve as source claim

definitions.definition: American Standard Code for Information Interchange; first 127 Unicode characters / Basic Latin.
A set of bit patterns designed to represent text symbols.

formulas.name: Color count from pixel bit depth
formulas.measures: Maximum distinct colors representable per pixel
formulas.interpretation: Each additional bit doubles the representable color set.
commonMistakes: Confusing bits per pixel with total image memory

sourceRefs.evidence: A color image uses 16 bits to represent a pixel. What is the maximum number of different colors

examples.title: Two-bit grayscale encoding
examples.scenario: Image uses gray scale with four levels.
reasoning: Assign 00, 01, 10, 11 to black, dark gray, light gray, white.
examples.lesson: Bit depth is determined by number of distinguishable values.

examples.title: 16-bit color image max colors
examples.scenario: Exercise 15: color image uses 16 bits per pixel.
reasoning: colors = 2^16
examples.lesson: Apply exponential growth of bit patterns, not linear count of bits.

comparisons.title: Forms of information
similarities: All ultimately need digital encoding for data communication.

confusions.correctDistinction: Source says numbers are converted directly to binary, not represented with ASCII.
confusions.examTrap: Assuming ASCII encodes numeric values for arithmetic.

sourceRefs.evidence: What is the maximum number of characters or symbols that can be represented by Unicode?

preservationRequirements: All five information forms with distinct representation rules.
Unicode 32-bit claim as stated + ASCII as Basic Latin.
Pixel bit-depth → color count formula with 16-bit exercise.

acceptable: Images are pixel matrices; more bits/pixel ⇒ more colors and more memory.
notAcceptable: Silently replacing source '32-bit Unicode' with UTF-8 without marking EXTERNAL_CONTEXT.

uncertainties: Unicode bit-width is a source claim; modern Unicode encodings differ — flag for CGP-2 if chapter needs accuracy notes.

topics.title: Data flow: simplex, half-duplex, full-duplex

sourceRefs.evidence: Communication between two devices can be simplex, half-duplex, or full-duplex.

learningObjectives: Classify a link as simplex, half-duplex, or full-duplex
Explain capacity use in each mode
Give device examples for each mode

concepts.title: Simplex
concepts.meaning: Unidirectional communication; only one of two devices can transmit; the other can only receive.

explanation.how: Entire channel capacity can be used to send data in one direction.
explanation.concrete: Keyboards and traditional monitors.
explanation.notMeaning: Not half of half-duplex; there is no reverse data path for the other device to send.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: One of three flow modes; direction/capacity details are exam favorites.

concepts.title: Half-duplex
concepts.meaning: Each station can both transmit and receive, but not at the same time.

explanation.what: Two-way, one direction at a time.
explanation.how: Entire capacity is taken over by whichever device transmits at the time.
explanation.concrete: Walkie-talkies and CB radios.
explanation.whenChanges: When both directions are never needed simultaneously, full capacity can be used per direction.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Review Q7 contrasts it with full-duplex.

concepts.title: Full-duplex (duplex)
concepts.meaning: Both stations can transmit and receive simultaneously.

explanation.how: Either two physically separate transmission paths, or capacity divided between directions.
explanation.concrete: Telephone network — both talk and listen at once.
explanation.whenChanges: Capacity must be divided between directions when a single medium is shared.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Third mode; capacity-sharing mechanism is a common deep question.

relationships.explanation: Half-duplex can dedicate entire capacity to one direction at a time; full-duplex must share capacity continuously.
Simplex never allows the receiving device to transmit on that link.

definitions.definition: Unidirectional communication on a link between two devices.
Each station can transmit and receive, but not at the same time.
Both stations can transmit and receive simultaneously (also called duplex).
definitions.qualifier: Capacity shared via two paths or divided link capacity

examples.title: Device examples per mode
examples.scenario: Map everyday devices to directionality models.
reasoning: Keyboard only inputs; monitor only outputs → simplex.
Walkie-talkie: one talks, other listens, then swap → half-duplex.
Telephone: simultaneous talk/listen → full-duplex.
examples.lesson: Classify by whether send and receive can occur simultaneously.

comparisons.title: Simplex vs Half-duplex vs Full-duplex
similarities: All involve two devices on a link.
comparisons.commonTrap: Calling half-duplex 'full two-way' without the simultaneity qualifier.

confusions.correctDistinction: Only full-duplex allows simultaneous transmit and receive.
confusions.examTrap: Choosing half-duplex when the scenario requires simultaneous talk/listen.

sourceRefs.evidence: Review Q7: difference between half-duplex and full-duplex.

preservationRequirements: Three modes with direction + capacity semantics + one device example each.
Half vs full simultaneity distinction.

acceptable: Half-duplex = two-way, not at the same time.

topics.title: Networks: definition, distributed processing, criteria

sourceRefs.evidence: A network is a set of devices (often referred to as nodes) connected by communication links.

learningObjectives: Define network and node
Explain distributed processing
State the three network criteria
Explain the throughput–delay tradeoff

concepts.title: Network
concepts.meaning: A set of devices (nodes) connected by communication links.

explanation.notMeaning: Not automatically the Internet; not automatically an internetwork.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Core definition; review Q11 contrasts network vs Internet.

sourceRefs.evidence: A network is a set of devices (often referred to as nodes) connected by communication links.

concepts.title: Node
concepts.meaning: Computer, printer, or any other device capable of sending and/or receiving data generated by other nodes.

explanation.what: Any communicating device on the network.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Terminology used in topology counts (n nodes).

concepts.title: Distributed processing
concepts.meaning: A task is divided among multiple computers; each handles a subset instead of one large machine owning all aspects.

explanation.why: Avoids single-machine responsibility for an entire process.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Review Q2 asks advantages of distributed processing.

sourceRefs.evidence: Most networks use distributed processing

concepts.title: Network criteria
concepts.meaning: The most important criteria a network must meet are performance, reliability, and security.
concepts.whyExamRelevant: Review Q3; missing from the current sample chapter.

sourceRefs.evidence: The most important of these are performance, reliability, and security.

concepts.title: Performance metrics
concepts.meaning: Transit time and response time; often evaluated as throughput and delay.

explanation.what: Transit time = message travel time device-to-device; response time = elapsed time between inquiry and response.
explanation.why: Performance depends on number of users, medium type, hardware capabilities, software efficiency.
explanation.whenChanges: Sending more data may increase throughput but also delay via congestion.
explanation.notMeaning: Performance is not only raw speed/bandwidth.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Throughput–delay contradiction is a classic conceptual item.

sourceRefs.evidence: If we try to send more data to the network, we may increase throughput but we increase the delay

concepts.title: Throughput
concepts.meaning: Networking metric of data successfully handled (desired higher).

explanation.what: One of two evaluation metrics named with delay.
explanation.whenChanges: Can rise with offered load, at cost of delay.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Paired with delay in tradeoff questions.

sourceRefs.evidence: Performance is often evaluated by two networking metrics: throughput and delay.

concepts.title: Delay
concepts.meaning: Networking performance metric of time cost (desired lower); increases under congestion.
concepts.whyExamRelevant: Tradeoff partner of throughput; exercise 23 is delay-sensitivity.

concepts.title: Reliability
concepts.meaning: Measured by frequency of failure, time to recover from a link failure, and robustness in a catastrophe.

explanation.what: Beyond accuracy of delivery — failure frequency, recovery time, catastrophe robustness.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: One of three criteria; often under-taught.

concepts.title: Security
concepts.meaning: Protect data from unauthorized access and damage; implement policies/procedures for recovery from breaches and losses.
concepts.whyExamRelevant: One of three criteria.

relationships.explanation: Often contradictory: more offered data can raise throughput and raise delay via congestion.
Depends on users, medium, hardware capabilities, software efficiency.

definitions.definition: A set of devices (nodes) connected by communication links.
Division of a task among multiple computers so each handles a subset.
Networking performance metric of data successfully transferred (often desired higher).
definitions.qualifier: Not defined as link bandwidth in this chapter

definitions.definition: Networking performance metric of time cost (often desired lower).

comparisons.title: Performance vs Reliability vs Security
similarities: All three are required criteria in the source.

confusions.left: bandwidth (not defined in this Ch.1 extract)
confusions.whyConfused: Sample chapter centers bandwidth; source centers throughput/delay.
confusions.correctDistinction: In this source, performance evaluation uses throughput and delay; bandwidth is not given a Ch.1 definition.
confusions.examTrap: Answering performance questions with a bandwidth-only story.

sourceRefs.evidence: Performance is inversely related to delay... more sensitive to delay?

preservationRequirements: Three criteria: performance, reliability, security.
Throughput–delay contradiction under load.
Distributed processing definition.

acceptable: More traffic can raise throughput and delay together.
notAcceptable: Higher bandwidth always makes every network faster (not source-stated here).

topics.title: Physical structures: connections and topologies

sourceRefs.evidence: There are two possible types of connections: point-to-point and multipoint.

learningObjectives: Distinguish point-to-point and multipoint connections
Classify mesh, star, bus, ring (and hybrid) topologies
Apply mesh link and port formulas
Explain advantages/disadvantages and failure modes of each basic topology

concepts.title: Link
concepts.meaning: A communications pathway that transfers data from one device to another.

explanation.how: Imagined as a line between two points for visualization.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Needed to count cables in topology exercises.

concepts.title: Point-to-point connection
concepts.meaning: Dedicated link between two devices; entire capacity reserved for those two.

explanation.how: Usually wire/cable; can be microwave or satellite.
explanation.concrete: Infrared remote establishing a connection to a TV control system.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Review Q4–Q5; prerequisite for mesh/star classification.

sourceRefs.evidence: A point-to-point connection provides a dedicated link between two devices.

concepts.title: Multipoint (multidrop) connection
concepts.meaning: More than two specific devices share a single link.

explanation.how: Capacity shared spatially (simultaneous) or temporally (turns).

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Prerequisite for bus topology; review Q4.

sourceRefs.evidence: A multipoint (also called multidrop) connection is one in which more than two specific devices share a single link.

concepts.title: Physical topology
concepts.meaning: Geometric representation of the relationship of all links and linking devices (nodes) to one another.
concepts.whyExamRelevant: Largest knowledge block; review Q6/Q8/Q9.

concepts.title: Mesh topology
concepts.meaning: Every device has a dedicated point-to-point link to every other device.

explanation.how: n(n−1)/2 duplex links; n−1 I/O ports per device.
explanation.concrete: Telephone regional offices needing mutual connectivity (limited mesh backbone).
explanation.notMeaning: Not the same as 'many links' without full connectivity.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Only source body formulas live here; exercises 9/16/17.

sourceRefs.evidence: In a mesh topology, every device has a dedicated point-to-point link to every other device.

concepts.title: Star topology
concepts.meaning: Each device has a dedicated point-to-point link only to a central controller (hub); devices are not directly linked.

explanation.how: Controller relays data between devices.
explanation.whenChanges: If hub dies, whole system dies (single point of failure).
explanation.concrete: High-speed LANs with central hub.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Common LAN topology; failure-mode questions.

concepts.title: Hub (central controller)
concepts.meaning: Central device in a star topology that acts as an exchange between stations.

explanation.what: Single point of dependency for star.
explanation.how: Can monitor link problems and bypass defective links while working.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Explains star advantages/disadvantages.

concepts.title: Bus topology
concepts.meaning: Multipoint topology with one long cable as backbone; nodes connect via drop lines and taps.

explanation.how: Signal weakens along the backbone (energy → heat); tap count/distance limited.
explanation.whenChanges: Break in bus cable stops all transmission; reflections create noise.
explanation.concrete: Early Ethernet LANs (less popular now per source).

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Line-configuration classification + failure analysis (ex. 17c, 20).

concepts.title: Drop line
concepts.meaning: Connection running between the device and the main bus cable.
concepts.whyExamRelevant: Bus anatomy vocabulary.

concepts.title: Tap
concepts.meaning: Connector that splices into or punctures the cable sheathing to contact the metallic core.

explanation.what: Physical connector onto the bus backbone.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Bus anatomy vocabulary.

concepts.title: Ring topology
concepts.meaning: Each device has dedicated point-to-point connections only to the two neighbors; signal passed along the ring; each device incorporates a repeater.

explanation.what: Closed loop with regeneration at each device.
explanation.how: Unidirectional traffic; dual ring or switch can mitigate breaks.
explanation.whenChanges: Simple ring break can disable entire network.
explanation.concrete: IBM Token Ring (historical prevalence).

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Failure modes and line configuration (ex. 6, 17d, 19).

concepts.title: Hybrid topology
concepts.meaning: Combination of topologies, e.g., main star with each branch connecting several stations in bus topology.

explanation.concrete: Star backbone with three bus networks.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Exercises 21–22 ask students to draw hybrids.

relationships.explanation: Mesh is built from dedicated p2p links between every pair.
Bus is the multipoint topology; star/mesh/ring use p2p links.
Hub failure kills the entire star system.
Each device regenerates bits via an internal repeater before passing them along.

definitions.definition: Dedicated link between two devices; entire capacity reserved for those two.
Connection in which more than two specific devices share a single link.
Geometric representation of the relationship of all links and nodes to one another.
Connection running between the device and the main bus cable.
Connector that splices into or punctures cable sheathing to contact the metallic core.
Central controller in a star topology that exchanges data between devices.

formulas.name: Fully connected mesh duplex links
formulas.measures: Number of duplex-mode physical links in a fully connected mesh
formulas.whenUsed: Cable/link count for mesh with n nodes
formulas.interpretation: Each of n nodes connects to n−1 others; each link counted twice, so divide by 2.

Answering ports when links were asked

sourceRefs.evidence: we need n(n-1)/2 duplex-mode links

formulas.name: Mesh I/O ports per device
formulas.measures: I/O ports required on each mesh device
formulas.whenUsed: Port-count questions for fully connected mesh
formulas.interpretation: Each device must reach the other n−1 stations.
commonMistakes: Giving cable count instead of port count

sourceRefs.evidence: every device on the network must have n - 1 input/output ports

examples.title: Six devices in mesh
examples.scenario: Exercise 16: six devices arranged in mesh topology.
reasoning: ports per device = n−1 = 5
examples.result: 15 cables; 5 ports needed on each device
examples.lesson: Compute links and ports separately; both use n but differently.

sourceRefs.evidence: Exercise 16: six devices mesh — cables and ports

examples.title: IR remote point-to-point
examples.scenario: Changing TV channels by infrared remote.
reasoning: Dedicated link between exactly two devices.
examples.lesson: Point-to-point is not only long-haul cable; short dedicated links count.

examples.title: Heterogeneous enterprise internetwork (topology angle)
examples.scenario: West office bus LAN; east office star LAN; president remote via WANs.
reasoning: Different topologies can coexist when interconnected.
examples.lesson: Topology choice is local; internetworking is global.

comparisons.title: Point-to-point vs Multipoint
comparisons.commonTrap: Calling a bus 'point-to-point' because each drop line is short.

comparisons.title: Mesh vs Star vs Bus vs Ring

values.star: less than mesh; may exceed ring/bus

values.mesh: robust; one link down does not incapacitate system
values.ring: simple ring break can disable network

similarities: All are basic physical topologies; hybrid combines them.
comparisons.commonTrap: Mixing mesh link count with star hub dependency.

applications.title: Telephone regional offices as limited mesh
applications.detail: Each regional office needs connection to every other regional office — practical limited mesh backbone.

applications.title: High-speed LAN star
applications.detail: Source: star topology is used in LANs; high-speed LANs often use star with central hub.

applications.title: Early Ethernet bus LANs
applications.detail: Bus was among first LAN topologies; Ethernet can use bus but less popular now (Ch.13 forward ref).

confusions.whyConfused: Both depend on n and appear in the same exercises.

topics.title: Categories of networks: LAN, WAN, MAN

sourceRefs.evidence: A LAN normally covers an area less than 2 mi; a WAN can be worldwide.

learningObjectives: Classify networks by size into LAN, MAN, WAN
Explain LAN resource sharing and typical topologies
Distinguish switched WAN and point-to-point WAN
Give MAN examples (DSL, cable TV)

concepts.title: LAN
concepts.meaning: Usually privately owned; links devices in a single office, building, or campus; currently limited to a few kilometers.

explanation.what: Local area network for resource sharing.
explanation.how: Share hardware/software/data among PCs/workstations; one machine may become server to clients.
explanation.concrete: Home office of two PCs + printer, or company LAN with audio/video peripherals.
explanation.notMeaning: Not defined primarily by brand of switch; size/ownership/scope matter.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Exercise 18 classification; review Q10.

sourceRefs.evidence: A local area network (LAN) is usually privately owned

concepts.title: WAN
concepts.meaning: Long-distance transmission of data/image/audio/video over large geographic areas (country, continent, world).

explanation.what: Wide area network spanning large regions.
explanation.concrete: Internet backbones; dial-up home line to ISP.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Core category; subtype distinction is exam-useful.

concepts.title: Switched WAN
concepts.meaning: WAN connecting end systems, usually comprising a router connecting to another LAN or WAN.

explanation.concrete: Early X.25; Frame Relay replacement; ATM with fixed-size cells.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Distinction from p2p WAN.

concepts.title: Point-to-point WAN
concepts.meaning: Normally a leased line from telephone/cable provider connecting a home computer or small LAN to an ISP.

explanation.concrete: High-speed DSL or cable modem line.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Connects end-user edge to Internet access story.

concepts.title: MAN
concepts.meaning: Network with size between LAN and WAN; normally covers a town or city; high-speed connectivity for endpoints across a city.

explanation.concrete: Telephone company high-speed DSL to customer; cable TV network used for data.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Middle category; often dropped when chapters only say LAN vs WAN.

sourceRefs.evidence: A metropolitan area network (MAN) is a network with a size between a LAN and a WAN.

relationships.explanation: Category is determined primarily by size: LAN < MAN < WAN.
LANs designed to share hardware, software, and data among workstations.

definitions.definition: Local area network: privately owned, links devices in a single office/building/campus; currently limited to a few kilometers.
definitions.qualifier: Distinguished by size, media, and topology

definitions.definition: Wide area network: long-distance transmission over large geographic areas.
Metropolitan area network: size between LAN and WAN, covering a town or city.

examples.title: MAN via DSL or cable TV
examples.scenario: City-scale high-speed connectivity examples from the source.
inputs: cable TV network upgraded for data
reasoning: Endpoints spread over a city need more than a building LAN.
examples.lesson: MAN is defined by geographic span, not a single technology.

examples.title: Home Ethernet hub classification
examples.scenario: Exercise 18: two computers connected by an Ethernet hub at home.
reasoning: Small privately owned local scope ⇒ LAN, not MAN/WAN.

comparisons.title: LAN vs MAN vs WAN

values.LAN: building/campus, a few km (source: often < 2 mi)

values.MAN: DSL city network, cable TV data

similarities: All are networks of nodes and links.
comparisons.commonTrap: Inventing precise speed tables not present in this source.

values.switched WAN: connects end systems via routers; backbone-like
values.point-to-point WAN: leased line from home/small LAN to ISP

confusions.correctDistinction: Size/ownership/scope decide category; a home Ethernet hub is a LAN.

preservationRequirements: LAN/MAN/WAN definitions by size/scope.
Switched WAN vs point-to-point WAN.
MAN examples DSL and cable TV.

acceptable: LAN is local and usually private; WAN spans large areas; MAN sits between.
notAcceptable: Invented Mbps comparison tables not in this source.

topics.title: Internetwork: connecting heterogeneous networks

sourceRefs.evidence: When two or more networks are connected, they become an internetwork, or internet.

learningObjectives: Define internetwork vs a single network
Explain the two-LAN + WAN heterogeneous scenario
Connect internetwork concept to the Internet

concepts.title: Internetwork / internet (lowercase)
concepts.meaning: Two or more networks that can communicate with each other.

explanation.what: Network of networks at any scale.
explanation.why: Rare to see LAN/MAN/WAN in isolation.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Review Q11; bridge to section 1.3.

sourceRefs.evidence: An internet (note the lowercase letter i) is two or more networks that can communicate with each other.

concepts.title: Heterogeneous enterprise mix
concepts.meaning: Different LAN topologies and WAN services joined into one internetwork.

explanation.how: Lease switched WAN backbone; attach sites with point-to-point WANs.
explanation.concrete: West bus LAN + east star LAN + president computer = 2 LANs + 4 WANs (Figure 1.12).

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Source's primary worked illustration of internetworking.

relationships.explanation: The Internet is the most notable internetwork.
Geographically separated LANs need WAN services to interconnect.

definitions.definition: Two or more networks that can communicate with each other.

examples.title: East/west offices + president remote
examples.scenario: Organization with two offices and a remote president.
reasoning: Lease a switched WAN backbone from a provider.
Connect each entity with a point-to-point WAN (DSL or cable modem).
examples.result: Heterogeneous network of four WANs and two LANs
examples.lesson: Internetworks compose different local designs via WAN services.

sourceRefs.evidence: Figure 1.12 A heterogeneous network made of four WANs and two LANs

comparisons.title: Network vs Internetwork
comparisons.commonTrap: Calling any single LAN an internet.

confusions.whyConfused: Colloquial use of 'the network' for the Internet.
confusions.correctDistinction: Network = devices+links; Internet = huge collection of interconnected networks.
confusions.examTrap: Defining Internet as 'a LAN with a router'.

sourceRefs.evidence: What is an internet? What is the Internet?

preservationRequirements: Internetwork definition with lowercase-i distinction.
Heterogeneous two-LAN + WAN scenario as the worked example.

acceptable: An internetwork is two or more connected networks.
notAcceptable: Equating every internetwork with the Internet.

topics.title: The Internet: history and ISP hierarchy

sourceRefs.evidence: The Internet is a structured, organized system.

learningObjectives: Summarize ARPANET timeline 1960s–1973
Explain TCP/IP split roles
Describe four-level ISP hierarchy with NAP/peering

concepts.title: The Internet
concepts.meaning: Uppercase-I Internet: collaboration of hundreds of thousands of interconnected networks.

explanation.what: Global internetwork used by individuals and organizations worldwide.
explanation.why: Structured system, not a random mesh.
explanation.notMeaning: Not government-run today (source: run by private companies).

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Core object of the chapter's third pillar.

sourceRefs.evidence: The most notable internet is called the Internet (uppercase letter I)

concepts.title: ARPANET history
concepts.meaning: ARPA/DoD-funded path from isolated mainframes (mid-1960s) to a four-node ARPANET in 1969.

explanation.how: Hosts attach to IMPs; IMPs interconnect; NCP for host communication.
explanation.concrete: Four nodes: UCLA, UCSB, SRI, University of Utah.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Dense factual timeline; high MCQ potential; absent from sample chapter.

concepts.title: IMP (Interface Message Processor)
concepts.meaning: Specialized computer attached to each host; IMPs connect to one another and to their hosts.

explanation.why: Allowed heterogeneous hosts to communicate via a common intermediate.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Supports ARPANET narrative.

sourceRefs.evidence: attached to a specialized computer, called an interface message processor (IMP)

concepts.title: TCP/IP split
concepts.meaning: TCP split into Transmission Control Protocol and Internetworking Protocol (IP).

explanation.what: Division of labor in the protocol stack origin story.
explanation.how: IP handles datagram routing; TCP handles segmentation, reassembly, error detection.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Foundational protocol architecture fact.

sourceRefs.evidence: IP would handle datagram routing while TCP would be responsible for higher-level functions

concepts.title: ISP hierarchy
concepts.meaning: International → national (backbones) → regional → local service providers.

explanation.what: Conceptual (not geographic) organization of today's Internet.
explanation.how: Most end users connect via local ISPs; local connect to regional or national.
explanation.notMeaning: Not a government hierarchy; private companies run it today.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Structural knowledge for 'how the Internet is organized today'.

sourceRefs.evidence: There are international service providers, national service providers, regional service providers, and local service providers.

concepts.title: NAPs and peering points
concepts.meaning: NAPs are third-party complex switching stations connecting national backbones; peering points are private interconnects between national ISP networks.

explanation.concrete: Source states peering points normally operate up to 600 Mbps.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Detail supporting ISP hierarchy.

relationships.explanation: NCP provided early host communication; TCP/IP later replaced it.
Today's Internet is organized via ISP layers and interconnects.

definitions.definition: The most notable internetwork: a collaboration of hundreds of thousands of interconnected networks (uppercase I).
Organization providing Internet connectivity; may be international, national, regional, or local.
Complex switching station (normally third-party) connecting national backbone ISPs.

examples.title: First ARPANET nodes (1969)
reasoning: Connect via IMPs; NCP for host-to-host communication.
examples.lesson: Internet began as a small research internetwork.

examples.title: TCP vs IP responsibilities
reasoning: IP: routing datagrams
TCP: higher-level functions
examples.lesson: Do not treat TCP and IP as synonyms.

comparisons.title: International vs National vs Regional vs Local ISPs

confusions.correctDistinction: Lowercase = any internetwork; uppercase = the global Internet.
confusions.examTrap: Using them interchangeably in definition questions.

sourceRefs.evidence: Compare the telephone network and the Internet.

preservationRequirements: 1960s–1973 timeline: ARPA, ARPANET, IMP, NCP, Cerf/Kahn, TCP/IP split with roles.
Four-level ISP hierarchy + NAP/peering.
Uppercase Internet vs lowercase internet.

acceptable: IP routes datagrams; TCP handles segmentation/reassembly/errors.
notAcceptable: Skipping history entirely; saying the Internet is 'just a big LAN'.

topics.title: Protocols: syntax, semantics, timing

sourceRefs.evidence: The key elements of a protocol are syntax, semantics, and timing.

learningObjectives: Define protocol with three key elements
Explain syntax, semantics, timing separately
Use the rate-mismatch example for timing

concepts.title: Protocol key elements
concepts.meaning: Syntax, semantics, and timing.

explanation.why: Rules must specify structure, meaning, and temporal behavior.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Review Q12; core definition depth beyond 'rules'.

concepts.title: Entity
concepts.meaning: Anything capable of sending or receiving information.
concepts.whyExamRelevant: Vocabulary for protocol discussion.

concepts.title: Syntax
concepts.meaning: Structure or format of the data — the order in which data are presented.

explanation.concrete: First 8 bits sender address, second 8 bits receiver address, rest message.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: One of three exam-asked elements.

sourceRefs.evidence: The term syntax refers to the structure or format of the data

concepts.title: Semantics
concepts.meaning: Meaning of each section of bits and the action to take based on that interpretation.

explanation.concrete: Does an address identify the route or the final destination?

concepts.whyExamRelevant: One of three elements; often confused with syntax.

concepts.title: Timing
concepts.meaning: When data should be sent and how fast they can be sent.

explanation.whenChanges: Sender faster than receiver ⇒ overload and data loss risk.
explanation.concrete: Sender 100 Mbps vs receiver 1 Mbps.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Third element; concrete rate example.

relationships.explanation: Syntax + semantics + timing together define what/how/when to communicate.
Protocol = rules; standard = agreed-upon rules for interoperability.

definitions.definition: Set of rules governing data communication; defines what is communicated, how, and when. Key elements: syntax, semantics, timing.

examples.title: 100 Mbps sender vs 1 Mbps receiver
reasoning: Production rate far exceeds processing rate.
examples.result: Transmission overloads the receiver; some data lost
examples.lesson: Protocols must address timing/rate, not only format.

examples.title: Simple header layout
reasoning: Syntax specifies presentation order of fields.
examples.lesson: Syntax is about structure/order of bits.

values.semantics: What does it mean / what action?

confusions.correctDistinction: Protocol governs communication; standard is an agreed-upon rule ensuring interoperation across manufacturers.
confusions.examTrap: Defining protocol as 'a document approved by ISO'.

sourceRefs.evidence: Why are protocols needed?

preservationRequirements: Always teach syntax/semantics/timing together.
Rate-mismatch timing example.
Protocol vs standard distinction preview.

notAcceptable: Protocol = just 'a set of rules' without the three elements.

topics.title: Standards, organizations, forums, Internet standards

sourceRefs.evidence: Data communication standards fall into two categories: de facto and de jure.

learningObjectives: Explain why standards are needed
Distinguish de facto and de jure
Name major standards organizations
Describe draft → RFC → Internet standard process

concepts.title: Why standards are needed
concepts.meaning: To ensure products from different manufacturers work together as expected.

explanation.what: Interoperability requirement in a heterogeneous vendor market.
explanation.why: Without standards, vendor products cannot reliably interconnect.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Review Q13.

concepts.title: De facto standards
concepts.meaning: Standards not approved by an organized body but adopted through widespread use.

explanation.how: Often established originally by manufacturers defining new product functionality.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Paired classification with de jure.

sourceRefs.evidence: De facto. Standards that have not been approved by an organized body

concepts.title: De jure standards
concepts.meaning: Standards legislated by an officially recognized body.
concepts.whyExamRelevant: Paired classification with de facto.

concepts.title: Standards organizations
concepts.meaning: ISO, ITU-T (formerly CCITT), ANSI, IEEE, EIA; plus forums and regulatory agencies such as FCC.

explanation.what: Bodies that create or influence standards.
explanation.concrete: ITU-T name change from CCITT on March 1, 1993; ANSI is private nonprofit, not US federal.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Factual MCQs on org roles; key-terms list includes them.

concepts.title: Forums
concepts.meaning: Special-interest groups of corporate representatives that evaluate and help standardize technologies faster than formal committees.

explanation.how: Work with universities/users; present conclusions to standards bodies.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Distinguishes forums from formal committees.

concepts.title: RFC and Internet standard process
concepts.meaning: Internet draft (working document, no official status, 6-month lifetime) may become a Request for Comment; RFCs have maturity levels and requirement categories.

explanation.how: Draft → RFC (edited, numbered, published) → maturity levels.
explanation.notMeaning: RFC does not automatically mean full Internet standard.

concepts.whyExamRelevant: Process knowledge; key term in glossary.

sourceRefs.evidence: An Internet draft is a working document... a 6-month lifetime.

relationships.explanation: Specification begins as draft, may become RFC, then Internet standard.
Forums speed evaluation and present conclusions to formal standards bodies.

definitions.definition: Standard established by widespread use rather than approval by an organized body.
Standard legislated by an officially recognized body.
Published specification in the Internet standards process; idea/concept precursor to an Internet standard.
definitions.qualifier: Goes through maturity levels and requirement categories

comparisons.title: De facto vs De jure
comparisons.commonTrap: Calling a popular product feature automatically de jure.

confusions.correctDistinction: Protocol is the communication ruleset; standard is the agreed/recognized specification enabling multi-vendor interoperation.
confusions.examTrap: Using the terms as perfect synonyms.

sourceRefs.evidence: Why are standards needed?
discuss the different types of RFCs

preservationRequirements: De facto vs de jure with definitions.
Major orgs ISO, ITU-T, ANSI, IEEE, EIA (+ FCC regulatory).
Draft → RFC → Internet standard process with 6-month draft lifetime.
Forums as accelerators, not replacements for committees.

acceptable: De facto = by use; de jure = by official body.
notAcceptable: Saying all Internet standards are de jure laws.
